Furthermore, how is it known that [phenomena] possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? The commentary states:
From here below is the fifth section, refuting the Sarvāstivādins and others who maintain that there are four real characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Within this, there are four parts; first, the question.
The opponent.
Next, the opponent’s response.
Third, the extensive refutation.
The fourth section sets forth the correct [position].
This shall be understood when we reach the passage below; this is the first [of those].
Treatise:
Because it is stated in the sūtras, up to and including the detailed exposition.
Commentary: [As follows].
This is the second instance in which an opponent cites a sūtra to prove that real characteristics exist.
Here, it should be stated that there are three characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). [The term] "conditioned" refers to...
Regarding the statement that "these characterized phenomena have three characteristics," this reveals that there are three characterizers (*lakṣaṇa*) for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
The repeated mention of "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) belongs to the characteristic of capability;
it reveals that phenomena possess this [nature].
Its essence is conditioned;
it is of the nature of dependent origination,
unlike the white heron.
The indicator signifies that water is not non-existent,
yet it is not like the physical marks of a young girl;
the indicated dharma is either wholesome or unwholesome.
It is not intended to emphasize that conditioned phenomena exist; rather, it expresses that conditioned phenomena do exist,
or that conditioned phenomena encompass both wholesome and unwholesome natures.
Now, in order to exclude this redundant expression "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*),
the word "this" (*idaṃ*) functions as a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*);
it is thus explained by the *tatpuruṣa* compound known as *taddhitārtha*.

Therefore, one should know that there is no statement that can be made regarding a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or essence (*svabhāva*) existing separately from the dharma itself, nor is there any distinct dharma [apart from it]. Question:
Since there are four characteristics, why does this sutra speak of only three? Regarding this, there are two explanations in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
The initial statement says "excluding abiding.
If a phenomenon causes conditioned factors to flow through the three periods of time,
the Sūtras describe this as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Arising (jāti) transfers future dharmas,
causing them to flow into the present;
change (jarā) and cessation (nirodha) transfer present dharmas.
They cause [the aggregates] to flow into the past,
so that they may wither, change, and perish—
just as three enemies, upon seeing their enemy in a forest, [pursue him].
They are dragged out, their strength withered;
their lives are destroyed.
They abide in the grasping of those dharmas and are established therein.
Pleasure is not dissociated [from its object].
Furthermore, among the characteristics [of conditioned phenomena], it is not said that they exist; moreover, unconditioned phenomena abide by way of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Because the characteristic of duration (sthiti-lakṣaṇa) would be confused with that [of permanence], the Sūtra does not mention it; however, when the Sūtra speaks of "duration and alteration" (sthity-anyathātva),
this is simply another name for this very characteristic of alteration (jarā).
Just as arising is called "origination" and cessation is called "extinction," so too, according to the second master,
within this very sutra, the combination of stability and change is called the characteristic of "stability-and-change."
"Abiding" (*sthiti*) is a state to which sentient beings are attached; therefore,
it is explained in conjunction with its opposite in order to induce revulsion,
just as when one points out that Kālī is accompanied by Śrī— this is explained at length.
That is to say, the arising of conditioned phenomena can also be understood,
as explained in the *Essential Points* (*Śāstramukha*). However, in the present Mahāyāna,
the textual explanations provided by those who interpret the sūtras differ from one another.
Some explain it as having one characteristic,
namely, taking "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" from among the four summaries (*uddāna*).
Others explain it as having two characteristics.
It means that the seal-disciples should contemplate all phenomena as abiding through arising and ceasing;
or as neither-arising-nor-ceasing within the "eight negations";
or as explained by the three characteristics.
Thus, in this sutra, three conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are taught, or sometimes four are taught.
Since they are identical in every instance, what is the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) for making such statements? Regarding the teaching of [only] one characteristic:
This means that the general designation "impermanence" refers to arising, ceasing, and so forth, because they possess the characteristic of non-eternality.
As it says in [Treatise] 81: "Because there is arising and passing away, this is impermanence."
That is to say, the combination of arising, ceasing, and so forth is termed "impermanence," as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (52): "If,
by means of these characteristics, one gives rise to contemplation of revulsion..."
It is taught merely as a characteristic that can give rise to weariness, detachment from desire,
and liberation.
That which was originally non-existent now comes into being;
having existed, it returns to non-existence—
this is called the characteristic of impermanence.

Therefore, the Sūtra states that "one" refers to impermanence itself. Why are arising, ceasing, and so forth collectively termed "impermanence"? Because there is no constant existence, and because there is no constant non-existence.
Non-existence is not eternally non-existent, which is why it is said to arise;
existence is not eternally existent, which is why it is said to cease.
That which is unconditioned exists as existence and is eternally existent.
Non-existence is eternally non-existent because it possesses two constant characteristics. However,
this conditioned existence is not eternal and is not identical to the unconditioned.
There is nothing that is not eternally non-existent and nothing that is not identical to a rabbit’s horn;
therefore, they are collectively termed "impermanent.
This is because there is no constant characteristic of non-existence apart from those [rabbit's horns].
This is not identical to the characteristic of cessation among the four [conditioned characteristics],
as it also includes arising. Because duration and change exist in the same temporal period as arising,
they are explained together when the two characteristics are discussed.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that arising (*jāti*) and change-in-duration (*sthity-anyathātva*) are manifested by their co-arising; therefore,
these two— duration and change— are combined into a single part.
The Chapter on Origination is established;
in the second part, the Chapter on Cessation is established.
This dharma is sometimes called the Chapter on Origination.
If that which is subsequently impermanent is called the category of cessation,
it causes all disciples to dwell in accordance with contemplation;
the eight negations do not reverse this.
To eliminate attachment, only two [aspects] are taught and no others.
Furthermore, the contemplation of revulsion that arises from the characteristic of impermanence is precisely the reason why these two are taught herein. As for the teaching of three characteristics:
Namely: first, arising;
second, cessation;
third, the alteration of duration.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are manifested by the three periods of time;
they arise from non-existence in the future."
Once it has arisen, it falls away into the past.

The phenomena of the present world are manifested by two characteristics, namely, duration (*sthiti*) and change (*anyathātva*); it is only for phenomena of the present that duration can be apprehended.
The changes occurring before and after also pertain only to the present;
these are collectively described as the single characteristic of "subsistence-and-change" (*sthity-anyathātva*),
which is similar to the explanation of the second master in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
However, since worldly conventions differ, those who explain the four characteristics do so because they employ four distinct meanings.
Nevertheless, the scripture cited here regarding the three characteristics is one universally accepted by all schools.
Treatise:
It is not established that this sutra fails to provide proof because it does not explicitly state [the point].
Commentary: [As follows:]
This is a general negation of the four characteristics of the Mahāyāna as being [identical to] matter, mind, and so forth.
It is neither identical nor different.
This negates the externalist position that there exists a distinct, substantially real self-nature;
therefore, it is said that this sutra does not speak of difference and so forth.
Below this, there are seven specific refutations. The treatise states:
It is not the case that the sixth consciousness reaches [its object] because it is identical to form and mind.
The commentary states:

First, regarding the objection that there is no difference between the six case-roles, [the author] refutes the statement concerning the sixth case-role cited by the opponent. The opponent formulates the following syllogism:
Regarding the statement that conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa) have a distinct substantial entity (svabhāva),
it is because there is a genitive case construction (ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti).
For example, Devadatta’s robe and Yajñadatta’s bowl;
now, an indeterminate fallacy is being raised on this basis.
Furthermore, as it is said in the world that the substance of form and mind does not exist as a separate substance apart from form and mind,
so too it follows that arising and the other [characteristics] likewise do not have a substance apart from the dharmas themselves.
That is to say, when one formulates a formal argument (*pramāṇa*),
the various phenomena (*dharma*) referred to by the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*) do not necessarily possess distinct substantial entities (*bhinnasvabhāva*).
Because it is the sixth transformation,
it is like the substance of form and mind,
such as the discernment of consciousness.
This does not negate that phenomena possess distinct intrinsic natures;
rather, it negates that arising and so forth necessarily exist as separate entities that are definitively contradictory [to their substrata]. The opponent objects:
The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is not identical to that which is characterized (*lakṣya*),
because they are spoken of as the "characteristic" and the "characterized."
Just as smoke indicates fire and so forth,
the same principle applies to the examples of the marks of a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa).
That is, the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and the characterized object (lakṣya) are each fixedly distinct from one another.
Therefore, it is known that arising (*jāti*) and so forth are distinct from the dharma itself. The Master of the Treatise refutes this, stating in the *Śāstra*:
"The essence of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) does not extend to other stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth."
The commentary states:
The second [point] is the objection that the subject and object are not distinct.
It is argued that the characteristics manifesting fire are distinct as subject and object.
For example, characteristics such as "arising" differ between subject and object;
whereas earth and so forth, or solidity and so forth, are one in both subject and object.
Thus, characteristics such as arising have no distinct substantial entity.
Although it is said that "earth has solidity as its characteristic" and so forth, up to "wind has motion as its characteristic," these are merely conventional expressions.
And as for the meanings of subject and object, they are not distinct in essence;
the same should apply to arising and so forth. However, according to what is commonly established, there is no such thing as a real mahāpuruṣa.
Since neither the Sautrāntikas nor the Mahāyāna scriptures accept [the existence of] a commonality of group (nikāya-sabhāga),
if one proceeds according to the perspective of others,
the Great Being (mahāsattva) is also established.
The Sarvāstivādins and others now cite the fact that the marks of a Great Being possess substantial reality according to their own school as an illustration;
this is done by relying on what is commonly accepted.
That analogy is not established;
therefore, in the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is countered with the objection:
"It is not the case that the marks of a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) are different from the Great Being himself."
In this context, the inference can be understood through its contrapositive.

However, when serving as a reason for another, it commits the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Here, the use of the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*) serves to exclude the possibility that [the effect] possesses a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This does not negate everything.
The opponent further says:
"If the essence of the characteristic and that which possesses the characteristic were one,"
Why does the Sūtra speak of the characteristics of the conditioned?
The Śāstra says:
If there were characteristics of the conditioned, they would have to be distinct from that which is characterized.
The commentary states:
Third is the "simultaneous refutation of the two aspects.
This is the challenge posed by the author of this treatise.
The Sūtra states that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has tranquility as its characteristic.
Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks of the characteristics of the unconditioned.
Therefore, there is no characterized object (*lakṣya*) distinct from its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
Your "unconditioned characteristic" must exist apart from its substance,
because you speak of it as a characteristic.

Just as the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) can be known through inference based on the conditioned itself, so too the reasoning of the present Master [Vasubandhu] should be understood in the same way;
for the Sūtra speaks of the characteristics of the conditioned.
One should establish its provisional characteristic separately;
since the Sūtra speaks of the characteristics of the unconditioned,
one should likewise establish its provisional characteristic separately.
Whether conventional characteristics are established or not,
the same applies to ultimate characteristics;
there are likewise those who maintain that they exist.
Because existence and non-existence exist, it is possible to establish provisional designations for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) based on their variations and distinctions.
Since the essence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not differ, what need is there to establish provisional characteristics? The unconditioned is without arising.
There is no aging and no cessation;
one should likewise establish these three characteristics of capability: that the essence is without arising or perishing.
Furthermore, it is not by means of multiple dharmas that distinct states are manifested;
therefore, unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) do not require the establishment of characteristics (lakṣaṇa).
This point should be reflected upon. The opponent further says:
The unconditioned does not fall into the world;
it does not conjoin with the conditioned. Since the conditioned has already fallen into the world, it is subject to conjunction.
Therefore, [the claim] that it conjoins with a capable [condition] is also incorrect.
That which is conditioned falls into the world;
what falls into the world conjoins.
The unconditioned is not of the world;
it does not conjoin with worldly phenomena.
The Mahāyāna should be thus.
The unconditioned is not of the world;
that which is not of the world has no provisional characteristics.
The conditioned falls within the world.
The objection that "falling into the world implies having no provisional characteristics" is not valid.
Characteristics are established for the sake of manifesting distinctions within the world;
unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) have no such internal distinctions.
How can provisional characteristics be established?
Furthermore, the *Śāstra* poses a further objection, saying:
Furthermore, regarding the statement that the characteristics such as arising arise simultaneously and exert their functions at once:
this is described as the fourth objection concerning the simultaneous arising of the four characteristics.
There are three sections.
First, the refutation that the example and the subject must both be subject to the same difficulty. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states:
"At the time of your production and activity..."
The three functions, such as abiding and so forth, should likewise arise immediately,
because they exist as actual entities,
just like the characteristic of arising (*jāti*). This is the case when the three dharmas— abiding and so forth— perform their functions.
The activity of arising ought to occur,
because it possesses an existing entity,
just like the three activities of abiding and so forth.
The same applies to the inference regarding the three functions, such as abiding;
for that school maintains that they arise sequentially.
Treatise.
"If [the functions] are contradictory, they cannot arise simultaneously.
The commentary states:
This is the second section of the subsection, providing an example of the refutation based on contradiction regarding their application.
This refers to the ancient Sarvāstivādins who maintained that functions arise sequentially; however,
the present author cites them because their [position on] functions is contradictory, and thus functions do not arise simultaneously.
Treatise:
Since their natures are mutually contradictory, how can they coexist?
Commentary: [It is said:]...
The author of this treatise raises an objection:

if the opponent should defend the position by saying that they can arise together because their essential natures (*svabhāva*) do not contradict one another, yet cannot coexist because their functions (*kāritra*) are contradictory; [the author replies:]...

One should immediately raise this objection: "Since the essence and its function are identical, their functions should likewise be mutually contradictory, because the essence is not separate from the function.
Conversely, since the function follows from the essence, the functions should not be contradictory."
Because it is not separate from its essence;
as with the essence, so it is here. Above this.
The ancient Sarvāstivāda masters raised this objection because the functions of the four characteristics arise separately at different times.
The masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* treatise sought to resolve this point.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
the functions of the three characteristics (trilakṣaṇa) all exist simultaneously;
it is only because their respective points of reference differ.
It abides in the induced outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Decay diminishes its power, causing subsequent results to be weaker than the preceding dharma;
its cessation may thus be known. This concludes the third section: the new school’s critique of the ancient tradition.
The author of the treatise refutes this. The treatise states:
Furthermore, the functions of subsistence, change, and cessation should not occur simultaneously.
The commentary states:
Because they are contradictory, like the feelings of suffering and pleasure. If they should offer this defense:
Who says they are contradictory?
If that were so, cessation would not be associated with [the mind],
because it is not contradictory to abiding.
As in the case of the characteristics of arising and so forth.
Furthermore, this master is challenged in the treatise.
"Because the characteristic and the characterized reach a state of non-distinct nature. Commentary:
The fifth section has three parts; first, the objection that [the characteristic] exists as its very substance from the beginning.
That school maintains that function exists apart from its substance;
therefore, they raise this objection [to show] that function must likewise exist inherently as being identical to the substance.
If he should offer this defense:
"Because it awaits causes and conditions, its activity does not arise instantaneously;
'causes' refers to the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and so forth."
Regarding "conditions," this refers to the other three conditions. Next is the second section: the objection that causes are not inherently existent, and the Master’s refutation thereof.
Treatise:
If it is argued that because their function reaches [the object], it must not be inherently present, the response is:
since this is already inherently present, why does it not arise all at once?
If the causes and conditions upon which [the effect] depends were non-existent beforehand,
it would contradict one's own tenets;
the same applies to the Master of the Treatise.
If the essence of the seed exists inherently,
why does it not constantly produce [its fruit]? If the essence of the seed does not exist inherently,
then logically there should be no seed at all.
If that which is provisional must depend on the conjunction of conditions to arise,
then the self, being real, must likewise depend on real conditions to arise.
If you truly exist dependent on conditions,
why do you not always combine with them?
If you exist falsely dependent on conditions, how can you be permanent?
"Why do they not arise all at once?
The explanation says:
"Because they are empty and insubstantial phenomena."
Although the seeds exist as conditions,
if there are no further external conditions, they cannot arise.
Because it is weak and inferior,
how can your "real dharma" be cited as an analogy?
This point should be reflected upon.
The Master of the Nyāyānusāra further defends this by saying:
"Because dharmas depend upon causes and conditions, they do not arise all at once;
for causes have degrees of proximity."
The same applies to conditioned phenomena (*dharmas*):
although a direct cause may exist,
it lacks the function of a remote condition.
Nor can it arise; for example,
although there may be a seed,
if the water does not coincide with the proper time.
Because the sprout does not arise,
the third section of the "Sub-section on the Seed" concerning the inability [of the seed] to produce [the sprout] is refuted by the Master of the Treatise.
Treatise:
Furthermore, it would follow that [the notions of] arising and so forth are useless.
Commentary: [This means:]...
Since the substantial cause consisting of its own kind already exists and other conditions also converge,
it has already attained birth.
Therefore, the adherence to [the existence of] arising and so forth is rendered useless.
Since water and seeds already exist, they must further depend on other factors for production;
thus, such arbitrary adherence to their substantial reality is indeed useless.
Treatise:
"The characterized is always existent... up to 'it also has arising,' etc.
Commentary states:
The sixth is the objection regarding the identity of essence and other characteristics.
Furthermore, since the characterized phenomena (lakṣya-dharma) exist eternally throughout the three times,
yet it is said that there is "arising" and so forth which come into conjunction with those phenomena.
If the unconditioned nature of yours were eternally existent,
it would necessarily be subject to conjunction with arising and so forth;
by this very logic, the unconditioned is established as being without arising and so forth.
The same should apply to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Herein, the logical inference (*anumāna*) can be understood through its application and its contrapositive.
Treatise.
Because mutually distinct causes cannot be found.
The commentary states:
If they were to offer this defense, saying that the dharmas of the three periods of time are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), [then...]
If it is conjoined with arising and so forth,
yet its unconditioned essence is eternally abiding,
how could there be arising and so forth?
The objection states:
"The essence of dharmas across the three periods of time is conditioned;
thus, it must possess the characteristics of the conditioned."
Since the essence of the unconditioned is eternally abiding, it should possess a conjunction with the characteristics of the unconditioned.
Furthermore, they offer this defense: conditioned phenomena have an arising that can be observed as being conjoined.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the unarisen (*anutpanna*) do not require conjunction.
An objection states:
"The unconditioned and the unarisen do not require conjunction."
Since conditioned entities arise [independently], why would they need to combine?
Because the critical examination based on such reasoning is inexhaustible,
the subsequent treatise states:
Because mutually distinct causes cannot be found.
"Cause" (hetu) means the reason (yoni).
[End of] Treatise.
Furthermore, the past and future worlds do not possess the nature of being substantially real.
[The author] states:
Regarding the seventh [point], there is no contradiction or difficulty concerning existence and non-existence.
There are two parts:
first, the objection; second, the conclusion.
Within the objection, there are four sub-sections.
First, regarding the difficulty concerning the existence or non-existence of the world:
to refute the non-existence of arising and ceasing,
one first refutes that the world does not exist.
The Pramāṇa states:
The two periods of past and future do not possess real substantiality.
Because they are not present and because they are not permanent,
like flowers in the sky and so forth.
These extraordinary words briefly clarify the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
This [unconditioned] certainly does not exist in the past or future.
Next is the second section: the refutation of the difficulty regarding arising and ceasing not being based [on the unconditioned].
Treatise:
Birth is called "existence" (bhava); it should therefore not be considered present.
Commentary: [This is stated].
That which is subject to arising is called "existent.
Since the future does not exist,
how can there be arising in that non-existent time?
Since the present exists,
the past is called non-existent;
the nature of cessation renders phenomena non-existent.
It would follow that it is not present;
thus, the characteristic of cessation would have to exist in the past.
However, the Sarvāstivādins state that it exists in the present.
He further attempts to rescue his position, saying:
"Who says that the nature of the characteristic of cessation is non-existent such that it would establish the past? [The author] replies: [This is not so].
"Cessation—if it were not non-arising, it would not exist.
Commentary: This is the third section of the "Son" [chapter], the refutation by reversing the characteristic of arising.
The author of this treatise raises an objection:
arising and ceasing are mutually contradictory in their essential natures;
the essence of an arisen phenomenon is existent.
Because cessation and arising are mutually contradictory,
the essence of the dharma of cessation becomes non-existent. If the essence of cessation were not non-existent, [it could not be cessation].
Birth would then not be existent; however, according to the masters of right reasoning (*nyāyavādin*),
birth possesses functional capacity (*samarthya*) in the future state.
Furthermore, that which exists in the past possesses the capacity to yield a fruit, but it does not possess activity;
activity belongs exclusively to the present,
which is precisely the function of grasping the fruit.
This is also not the case.
Why? Because it would follow that all dharmas of going and coming would possess causal efficacy (*samarthya*), whereas arising (*jāti*) is not an activity (*kāritra*).
Furthermore, since giving a fruit is not itself an activity,
it would follow that all future dharmas should arise at all times,
and all past dharmas should constantly give their fruits.
If it is said that "activity" refers to the present,
while "capacity" refers to the past and future,
then it follows that the present possesses capacity.
It should be called "past" and "future.
Only the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) can be termed "activity" (*kāritra*) because it grasps its fruit;
the characteristics of change (*anyathātva*) and cessation (*nirodha*) cannot grasp a fruit.
This would mean that it is merely a functional capacity and thus not present.
If one were to argue that activity does not necessarily involve the grasping of a fruit, [the response follows].
This clearly demonstrates that the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) is likewise not a functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).
This point should be examined;
it is not found in any of the treatises.
Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle three, that the three dharmas of the future possess functional activity (*kāritra*),
how is this further reconciled with the treatise?
Furthermore, regarding the cessation of that which contradicts abiding, to what extent can there be a difference in time?
The commentary states:
This is the fourth sub-section, the objection that what is contradictory must necessarily differ.
Furthermore, cessation and the dharma that is ceased,
as well as duration and the dharma that endures,
are in their very nature mutually contradictory.
It is better to maintain that [the cause] belongs to the same world-system; since its abiding does not contradict its arising,
it causes the phenomenon to exist as a single type.
How could it be possible for [the characteristics] to belong to different time periods? Therefore, arising (*jāti*) and duration (*sthiti*) must both exist in the present;
the characteristic of cessation (*anityatā*), being non-existent in substance, causes [the dharma] to become past.
Cessation must necessarily differ from abiding in the world;
therefore, the arguments for and against their position are irrational.
The commentary states:
The second [point] is a summary of the refutation;
to proceed further would be contradictory.
Their substance cannot coexist;
once they have regressed, they do not revert.
Why then would their functions not arise simultaneously?
Furthermore, advancing [to a higher state] would be illogical,
as cessation and abiding could not occur simultaneously; retreating [to a lower state] would likewise be illogical.
Arising and abiding should likewise belong to the same time period;
furthermore, if abiding and cessation were to belong to different time periods,
it would contradict your own tenets.
To retreat and remain [in that state] is to destroy the commonality of the world;
furthermore, it deviates from correct principle.
A separate refutation of the distinct characteristics is as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Thus, the prior [state] would not be established as different;
being different from the prior, it would not be a single dharma.
The detailed explanation is as in that [text].
For now, I shall not analyze this in detail.
However, regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), there are four conventionally established characteristics (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states:
The following section sets forth the author's own position; this text consists of two parts.
First, the presentation of the author's own position.
The subsequent section concludes with the provisional [position], while the initial section sets forth the correct meaning.
This text further consists of five parts;
first, it distinguishes the intent of establishing the characteristics as taught by other schools.
The meaning of the text is clear. The treatise states:
"That which was originally non-existent and now exists, until the time it becomes non-existent again, is called 'cessation'."
The commentary states:
From here below is the second section, which explains the characteristics and manifestations of the marks.
Regarding the "four marks," these refer to phenomena such as that which was originally non-existent but now exists, and so forth.
The suspension [of activity] is called "abiding.
It is distinct from the preceding and succeeding moments of phenomena;
thus, arising and ceasing can be known.
This is all as explained in the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
